gen-dafont-disorder-gf-noto-sans-mro: Disorder looks like bent paperclip wire, every joint left bare with no swelling where curves meet stems. Noto Sans Mro goes the other way, its words dense and tall through the middle, so a long page of it settles into a steady, modern texture.
gen-dafont-disorder-gf-noto-sans-multani: Noto Sans Multani has a lofty x-height and an e with a wide gap at its terminal, which gives it a bright, open face. Disorder is raw by comparison, flat in line weight, and if it were shrunk down its spaced-out letters would lose their bite.
gen-dafont-disorder-gf-noto-sans-myanmar: Noto Sans Myanmar reads thick and heavy through the middle of each line, with a c that opens broadly. Disorder, up top, has no thick-thin swing at all, just raw, chaotic letters set well apart from one another.
gen-dafont-disorder-gf-noto-sans-nabatae: Tall and a little wild. Disorder pairs diagonals as thick as its horizontals with Noto Sans Nabataean, whose lowercase nearly reaches cap height and whose s curves sit wide open, and that mix of raw and crisp is the real draw.
gen-dafont-disorder-gf-noto-sans-nag-mun: Noto Sans Nag Mundari has c and s shapes that look half unwrapped, and a lowercase that rivals its capitals in size. Disorder is the rawer partner, its curves meeting stems with no swelling, so a size bump for the body would make little sense.
gen-dafont-disorder-gf-noto-sans-nandina: Disorder arrives chaotic and raw, its diagonals as thick as its horizontals, every glyph pushed away from the next. Noto Sans Nandinagari is the approachable half, with short ascenders, a big lowercase body, and openings that stay generous at every weight.
gen-dafont-disorder-gf-noto-sans-newa: Disorder is all joints, strokes meeting without thinning or bulging, and the result feels chaotic and a bit raw. Noto Sans Newa does the quieter job of keeping its lowercase e clearly open, with tall counters and bowls that stay easy on the eye.
gen-dafont-disorder-gf-noto-sans-nushu: Raw letters, towering lowercase. Disorder holds its strokes at the fixed pressure of a stylus, and Noto Sans Nushu answers with terminals held far from the stroke body, so a modern, airy openness is what they have in common.
gen-dafont-disorder-gf-noto-sans-ogham: Noto Sans Ogham looks bold for its weight, since its tall lowercase bodies fill the line and its e keeps a wide gap. Disorder, with no difference between up and side strokes, feels rawer beside it.
gen-dafont-disorder-gf-noto-sans-ol-chik: Glass tubing bent into letters, that is Disorder, chaotic and raw. Noto Sans Ol Chiki holds the tails of its curves well back from the body, so its words read as solid, clean blocks rather than skylines over a whole page.
